rationale: A wins because it keeps the story inside the fence of the facts: "A 22% drop in no-shows: what Mindbody's AI pilot proves and what it doesn't" is exactly the right level of skeptical trade-story framing. B has ambition, but it starts writing checks the update can't cash; "Mindbody's AI treats 50,000 studios' booking calendars as one data set" is a great story only if true, and the update does not say that. A gives a founder usable press strategy; B needs a fact-check leash before it leaves the room.
gaps_in_A: A leaves a careful ClassPass/platform-power angle mostly on the table; "Does the assistant fill freed spots from the studio's own waitlist only, or does ClassPass inventory come into play?" is treated only as a risk question, not as a bounded structural story.
"or a small-business columnist at a regional business outlet" is only viable if there is a named local pilot studio. Without that, it is a little too broad for the customer-story angle.
"A reporter can test whether this is a retention move" is smart, but retention is still an inference. The angle should keep that hypothesis visibly conditional all the way through.
gaps_in_B: "Mindbody's AI treats 50,000 studios' booking calendars as one data set" is invented. The update says Mindbody has scale and uses booking data; it does not say it pools 50,000 calendars into one data set.

"Mindbody owns the software studios run on and the marketplace that fills their classes — and it's adding AI to both" overclaims. The update says the assistant is for scheduling; it does not say AI is being added to ClassPass.
"The AI upgrade boutique fitness startups promised just shipped from the incumbent instead" invents the startup challenger frame. No competitor, challenger, or promise appears in the update.
"private-equity ownership" and "PE-owned SaaS companies" go beyond the supplied facts. The update says privately held after a take-private deal; name the owner or keep the PE frame out.
